item.title: Generalizing and Combining Check Constructions: Design-Space Exploration for Fault-Tolerant Quantum State Preparation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Block Checks and Pareto tree search find post-selected CSS state preparation circuits with fewer operations at the depth of every published circuit. At depth 7, the [[25,1,5]] surface code uses 91 operations and 16 auxiliary qubits instead of 262 and 63.

Grade 0.524 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Ludwig Schmid, Robert Wille

Figure

Total operations broken down by circuit component across the Pareto front of depth for [[17,1,5]] color and [[25,1,5]] surface codes, compared against published circuit points.

Asks

How can post-selected fault-tolerant quantum state preparation circuits systematically explore and optimize trade-offs between circuit depth and operation count?

Before

Prior Steane-type check circuits for [[25,1,5]] required 262 operations and 63 auxiliary qubits at depth 7 (Weilandt et al. 2024).

But

CSS codes with distance d≤7. Search runtime scales poorly beyond distance 7 or 9. Logical error rates under p=10−3 circuit-level depolarizing noise can be up to three times higher than baseline circuits due to unoptimized weight-(t+1) faults.

Tools

Block Checks · Pareto tree search · Stim Monte Carlo simulations · Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT)

Code. https://github.com/munich-quantum-toolkit/qecc

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs logical states prepared such that single faults cannot spread into uncorrectable errors. Post-selection achieves this with added checks that detect dangerous faults and discard the run. How the checks are measured sets the depth and operation count of the circuit, and the best trade-off depends on the hardware. Existing automated methods, however, each use one check construction and yield fixed trade-offs. We first introduce Block Checks, in which several checks share one fault-tolerantly prepared auxiliary block, which places them and existing constructions in a single design space. Second, to explore that space, we propose a Pareto tree search that adds checks and auxiliary blocks, merges auxiliaries, and edits the circuit. On quantum codes of distance up to seven, the search finds best-known circuits for many new operation--depth trade-offs and surpasses existing methods. The code is open source as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT) at https://github.com/munich-quantum-toolkit/qecc, and all circuits are available in the QECirc library at https://qecirc.com.

item.title: Stitching Quantum Codes into Quilts: Universal Logic with no Ancillary Qubits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Measures joint logical Pauli products between QLDPC and surface codeblocks using a subsystem code quilt with zero ancilla data qubits and no extra measurement qubits beyond those for idle syndrome extraction. Circuit logical error rates match idle memory at physical error rates p=1.5×10−3 to 3×10−3 for the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle and distance-12 rotated surface codes.

Grade 0.509 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Stasiu Wolanski

Figure

Total circuit failure probability plotted against circuit physical error rate p. Subsystem protocol quilt circuits maintain logical error rates comparable to baseline idle memory circuits on distance-12 rotated surface and 144-qubit bivariate bicycle codes.

Asks

Can fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between QLDPC codes be executed without ancillary codeblocks, extra physical qubits, or severe time overhead?

Before

Generalized surgery required ancillary 'logical processing units' of roughly half the codeblock size and incurred an approximate 20× time overhead (Yoder et al. 2024).

But

Subsystem gauge-measurement protocol is provably non-fault-tolerant in the asymptotic large-distance limit. Evaluated under standard uniform depolarizing circuit noise via numerical Monte Carlo simulation; decoder requires seconds per shot.

Tools

Subsystem code quilts · Detector error model folding · Branch-and-bound circuit-distance finder · Relay-BP decoding with GARI-style multi-presentation corroboration

Abstract

Proposals abound for performing fault-tolerant logical Pauli-product measurements between quantum codes beyond the surface code. We introduce a new construction, the code quilt, whereby a target joint logical operator of two or more codeblocks is directly measured without the use of an ancillary system. We construct explicit circuits to perform a logical measurement using the quilt construction, which also require no physical qubits beyond the ancillas already in place to perform idle syndrome extraction on the codeblocks in question. We give a detailed structural analysis of the construction, which is based on a subsystem code, and provide several sets of sufficient conditions under which the relevant code-capacity distance is preserved. We give two variants of the protocol. The first, where the gauge generators of the subsystem code are measured directly, is provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but admits a particularly practical circuit implementation in which the physical qubit degree increases by at most two. The second has more favourable asymptotic properties, although we do not prove its fault tolerance in the general case. We then perform an extensive empirical analysis of the technique, in particular of the first variant, as applied to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, finding code-capacity-distance preserving quilts for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators. We optimise to find sparse and decongested detector bases for each and, for a randomly selected subset, find circuits that we estimate to be distance preserving. Finally, we perform decoding experiments on a subset of these circuits and find that their logical error probability is comparable to that of idle memory for operations involving the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between 1.5×10⁻³ and 3×10⁻³.

item.title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Rapids decodes distance-19 surface-code syndrome rounds in under 1 microsecond on a single FPGA with 20 microseconds latency, achieving a 240 times lower logical error rate than real-time union-find decoders.

Grade 0.507 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold” · Chenyang Jin, Susanne F. Yelin, Andi Gu

Figure

Logical error rate versus throughput (c), error suppression factor Λ (d), and latency across code distances (e) for surface-code memory experiments at p=0.15% under SI1000 noise, comparing Rapids against prior real-time decoders.

Asks

Can a classical decoder keep pace with sub-microsecond syndrome cycles of superconducting quantum processors without sacrificing decoding accuracy or suffering high decision latency?

Before

Neural decoders could not exceed distance-11 at 1 microsecond throughput, or had latencies reaching 1 ms (AlphaQubit 2 RT); dedicated real-time hardware decoders sacrificed accuracy and reached at most distance-7 (or distance-11 with high error rates).

But

Evaluated primarily in simulation under SI1000 circuit-level noise; chip-to-chip latency floor modeled based on RTL simulation with Aurora links.

Tools

streaming convolutional neural network with GRU · FPGA co-design (AMD Versal VP1802) · quantization-aware training (4-bit/8-bit integer) · Monarch matrix layers · depthwise separable convolutions

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

item.title: Structure-Guided Synthesis of Low-Error Syndrome Extraction Circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Relative to Auto-Stabilizer-Check (ASC), median logical error rate (LER) drops by 11.4% (up to 38.6%) across 15 qLDPC codes, with time to first feasible circuit accelerating by factors of 21.4 to 136.6.

Grade 0.486 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Shanchuan Li, Xin Hong, Pengcheng Zhu, Xiangzhen Zhou, Fanxu Meng, Shenggang Ying

Figure

Logical error rate (LER) versus physical error parameter p (0.001 to 0.005) for five codes. Solid curves for the structure-guided synthesis consistently sit below dashed curves for ASC.

Asks

How can recurring code connectivity be leveraged to synthesize low-depth, low-logical-error-rate syndrome extraction circuits without combinatorial explosion?

Before

Auto-Stabilizer-Check (ASC) independently solves per-check orderings via constraint satisfaction.

But

Evaluated on 15 structured CSS qLDPC codes under superconducting-inspired SI1000 circuit-level noise; requires code construction representations (such as polynomials or group algebras) to identify recurring check connectivity.

Tools

CP-SAT solver · Stim detector error models · Telescoping decoder · dist_m4ri distance calculator

Abstract

Gate orders can change fault propagation and logical error rates even when syndrome-extraction circuits implement the same ideal stabilizer measurements. Optimizing these orderings independently for every check, however, becomes computationally demanding as code size increases. We present a synthesis method for structured Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes that groups checks by recurring connectivity and shares one relative gate order per group, reducing independent ordering choices. A CP-SAT solver jointly determines the shared orders and the execution time of each physical gate, enforcing resource and measurement constraints across the circuit. Noisy circuit simulations with decoding then guide the selection of the final circuit. We compare with state-of-the-art approaches, including Auto-Stabilizer-Check (ASC), PropHunt, and AlphaSyndrome. Across 15 quantum low-density parity-check codes from ten code families, our method achieves the lowest logical error rate estimates. Relative to ASC, the strongest baseline in our evaluation, the median reduction is 11.4% and the largest is 38.6%. Our circuits improve circuit-level distance over ASC on ten instances and preserve the code distance in seven. Across five timed codes, our method reduces the mean time to the first feasible circuit by factors of 21.4-136.6 relative to ASC, at equal or lower depth.

item.title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Non-binary detector error models reduce Tanner graph edges by 4.3 to 5.3× and 4-cycles by 9 to 13×, lowering logical error rates under belief propagation while accelerating BP with OSD by up to 9.4× on a CPU.

Grade 0.483 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Stefano Tinelli, Francisco Lázaro, Francisco García Herrero

Figure

Logical error rate (LER) versus physical error rate p comparing binary (dashed) and non-binary (solid) DEMs under flooded belief propagation with and without OSD post-processing across surface, color, and bivariate bicycle codes.

Asks

Can syndrome extraction circuit noise be decoded more effectively by representing each fault location with a single non-binary random variable over its native alphabet rather than decomposing it into independent binary mechanisms?

Before

Standard binary detector error models generated by Stim decompose non-binary Pauli channels into independent Bernoulli mechanisms, creating numerous 4-cycles inside fault locations.

But

Circuit-level Pauli noise on Clifford circuits; verified on d=5 rotated surface code, d=5 6.6.6 color code, and [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code; parallel flooded scheduling with max 100 iterations.

Tools

split-merge-regroup transformation · scalar-message non-binary belief propagation · ordered statistics decoding (OSD-CS) · Stim circuit simulation

Code. https://github.com/s-tinelli/nbdem

Abstract

A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to 9.4× faster in a CPU.

item.title: The Clifford Hierarchy from Clifford Stabilizers in 2D
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — 2D topological codes with Clifford stabilizers can realize transversal logical Ck−1Z gates at arbitrary level k of the Clifford hierarchy using depth-one physical circuits of Pauli Z or CZ gates.

Grade 0.476 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Alison Warman, Sakura Schafer-Nameki

Figure

Quantum circuits implementing the Clifford stabilizers and the two transversal non-Clifford logical gate schemes: a depth-one line of single-qubit Z gates (Ue) and a depth-one layer of two-qubit CZ gates (Mpα).

Asks

Can 2D topological qubit codes with Clifford stabilizers realize constant-depth logical gates beyond level 3 of the Clifford hierarchy?

Before

All known 2D topological qubit codes placed constant-depth logical gates at most one level above their stabilizers (level 𝒞(ℓ+D−1), giving level 3 for Clifford stabilizers ℓ=2), leading to a conjectured general bound.

But

Constructed on an L×L square lattice patch; logical Ck−1Z gate requires k≥3; physical circuits assume ideal operations without error decoding implementation.

Tools

Kitaev quantum double codes of D₄^(k_A-1)×Z₂ · gapped boundary engineering · non-Abelian anyon crossings · depth-one Z and CZ physical gate layers

Abstract

The Bravyi-König theorem limits the constant-depth logical gates of 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes to be in the Clifford group. Known qubit codes with Clifford stabilizers exceed it by only one level of the Clifford hierarchy, and this was conjectured to hold generally. We show that this bound can be completely bypassed, and that topological codes with Clifford stabilizers in 2D can realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy. We present two explicit constructions of codes based on copies of the quantum doubles of D₄ and Z₂, with k logical qubits and a logical C^(k-1)Z gate, which is at level k of the Clifford hierarchy. The physical circuits realizing the gates consist only of physical Z or CZ gates. The main new ingredient comes from the logical encoding, which depends crucially on non-Abelian group multiplication.

item.title: Ellis: Extremely Fast Quantum Circuit Simulation under Qubit Loss and Leakage
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Ellis simulates frame-CSS quantum circuits under qubit loss and Pauli noise via masked Pauli-frame sampling, reaching 952,000 shots per second on the BB144 gross code using a single CPU core.

Grade 0.473 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Yuewen Hou, Gokul Subramanian Ravi

Figure

Parity outcomes of a two-qubit circuit before and after qubit loss. Dropping a CX gate changes the detector matrix and fixed parity check.

Asks

Can Clifford circuits subject to qubit loss and leakage be simulated with a single common reference measurement record instead of per-shot tableau simulation?

Before

Clifft in online mode and PPVM tableau simulations required per-shot updates; Ellis is about three orders of magnitude faster than Clifft and four orders faster than PPVM.

But

Circuits must be frame-CSS (single-qubit Pauli-basis resets and readouts, single- and two-qubit Clifford gates, no classically controlled gates); relies on the gate-cancellation loss model without reloads at reset.

Tools

masked Pauli-frame simulation · union-find frame certification · gate-cancellation loss model · tableau simulation

Abstract

Qubit loss and leakage are persistent errors: while a qubit remains lost or leaked, every operation acting on it is dropped. Consequently, the Clifford circuit executed differs from shot to shot. This variation breaks Pauli-frame simulation, which constructs each shot by XORing sampled Pauli flips onto a single emphcommon reference measurement record. By rethinking the roles of tableau simulation and Pauli-frame simulation, we show that many key fault-tolerant primitives nevertheless retain a common reference under loss. These include CSS code memory, lattice surgery, and transversal CNOT. Such circuits can therefore be simulated exactly under Pauli noise and loss by a Pauli frame with per-shot masks for the dropped operations. We define emphframe-CSS circuits as those that are CSS up to local single-qubit basis changes, given a loss model that specifies where qubits can be lost and reloaded. We prove that every frame-CSS circuit has a common reference, and we give a practically near-linear-time procedure that certifies whether a circuit is frame-CSS. We implement the certifier and a high-performance simulator in the open-source package hrefhttps://github.com/isaachyw/ELLIStextscEllis (Efficient Loss and Leakage Invariant-reference Simulation). On the gross code under qubit loss and Pauli errors, ellis samples 952,000 shots per second on a single CPU core, at least 1000× faster than Clifft~citechase2026 and PPVM~citeluo2026ppvm.

item.title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — In-place integer modular multiplication modulo a power of two, standard integer multiplication, and modular inversion modulo a power of two run in O(n1+ϵ) gates for any ϵ>0 with zero ancilla qubits (or ⌈log2⁡m⌉ ancillas for standard multiplication by a general quantum multiplier).

Grade 0.457 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · David Halpenny, Adithya Sireesh, Petros Wallden

Figure

The plot displays the number of modular multiplications required to perform in-place inversion modulo 2m as the number of clean ancilla qubits s increases.

Asks

Can in-place and ancilla-free quantum arithmetic algorithms achieve subquadratic gate complexity?

Before

Existing in-place, ancilla-free integer multiplication and modular multiplication algorithms required Ω(n2) gates.

But

Multipliers restricted to odd integers for modular operations and non-zero integers for standard multiplication; registers sized with m=O(n); small ϵ introduces large constant factors.

Tools

phase-encoded fast integer multiplication · controlled and parametrized quantum Fourier transform · abstract quantum circuit model

Abstract

Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block in the design of quantum algorithms, with their implementation cost expected to have a significant impact on the viability of a wide variety of quantum applications. In this work, we present novel algorithms for a number of in-place quantum arithmetic operations that are highly efficient in terms of their space and gate count overheads compared to the current state-of-the-art. We show that in-place modular multiplication of integers, modulo a power of two, can be performed with either a classical or quantum odd multiplier using O(n^(1+ε)) gates and no ancilla qubits, for any ε>0. We then show that standard in-place integer multiplication can be performed with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier using O(n^(1+ε)) gates for any ε>0, with no ancilla qubits required for the classical multiplier and a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits for the quantum. Using our quantum modular multiplication algorithm, we also show that in-place modular inversion, modulo a power of two, can be performed using O(n^(1+ε)) gates and no ancilla qubits, for any ε>0. To our knowledge, these are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of these fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, only requiring enough space to store the output of the operation, which overwrites the input directly. We present our multiplication algorithms as consequences of a single unified theorem, which may find further application within quantum arithmetic.
